title: Show HN: ccfleet, a quiet, tmux-native Claude Code dashboard
text:
At work, we're leaning heavily into agentic development. I've always used tmux to manage my work and now I'm using it to organize my 30+ Claude sessions.

I wanted a simple read-only dashboard that would identify which of my sessions needed attention and also fit my vim-based navigation workflows. There are times when all I remember is a name or phrase from a conversation. The search feature was built to address this by searching the contents of every transcript, not just session titles.

Just curious if other devs are experiencing similar issues and whether this approach is helpful at all. Thanks!

title: Show HN: Sheetgraph, AI agents can understand complex spreadsheets
text:
Hi guys,

I built a tool www.lovespreadsheets.com earlier this year and a huge problem we kept running into is processing messy, real-world, complex spreadsheets for AI agents.

Even a "medium" sized spreadsheet converts to about 1m+ tokens if read fully, which immediately blows up the current context windows of most models. So I noticed most agents sample data from spreadsheets in chunks instead.

So I (& Claude) built this library Sheetgraph, https://github.com/asharma327/sheetgraph, to compress spreadsheets (~100x compression) while still maintaining their structure (like a dependency graph for formulas) & other relevant metadata such as macros, cell data types, formatting. There is a zipped full workbook of the spreadsheet as well for the agent to lookup data as needed.

Still rough around the edges so would love any feedback on both the idea and any details. This is used in our primary product + services platform Love Spreadsheets so we are actively maintaining and improving it.

Thanks!

title: Show HN: Fast agentic video editing in the browser (Tella)
text:
Hi HN, today we're launching the biggest update to Tella ever (https://tella.com/).

Tella is all-in-one video creation. You can record, edit and publish with one tool. Today we're shipping:

1. Tella Agent: An in-app video editing agent 2. Tella Motion: Rich motion graphics support 3. Auto Capture: Agentic screen recording

Our in-app agent uses the same tools as our MCP. All year we've been exposing more of our editor to the MCP. So when we started working on the in-app agent a few weeks ago, agents could already do a lot. Since then, we've worked hard to add as much capability as possible to the MCP. So whether you're editing on tella.com or from Claude Code you get the same capabilities.

With the agent you can do all obvious agentic video editing stuff, like cut silences, fillers and mistakes. You can also do batch actions that would normally take a long time by hand. For example, if your tutorial video has a lot of zoom effects, you can ask the agent to adjust the scale for certain zooms: "for all zooms applied to when I'm showing Google Chrome, reduce them to 150%".

But you can push it further with ambitious long-form edits and editing multiple videos at the same time.

LLMs have proven to be very good at motion graphics. Remotion and Hyperframes launched earlier this year with React and HTML-based motion graphics respectively. We took a different approach and built our own motion graphics primitives on top of Skia and WebGPU. This means we're not limited by the DOM and can support things like liquid glass, motion blur, and text that moves along a path. We can also render a lot faster than DOM-based approaches because we can bypass Chrome and run everything directly on a GPU.

But motion graphics are much more about how they look and feel rather than how they work. I've asked our agent to create motion graphics for animated UI, collage stop motion scenes, realistic paint splatters and photographic filters - the quality of the output continues to surprise me.

Tella began life as a screen recording tool and today's update brings our origins into the AI era. Auto Capture is our new agentic screen recording tool. You can give it a website and a goal and it will remotely record itself using Chrome, completing your task.

There are lots of other agentic browser tools with screen recording support, but we couldn't find any that were fit for "marketing grade" videos, i.e. recordings done in 4K at 60fps. So we built our own.

For this to be practical (i.e. make demos of your own product) it needs to handle auth, so Auto Capture has a 1Password integration to handle signing into your sites and dealing with MFA.

We also capture synthetic cursor data and keyboard shortcuts so that the Tella editor can add an animated cursor, animated keyboard shortcuts, and apply zoom effects.

You can try all of this in your browser or connect to our MCP.

Let me know what you think.

Announcement + video here: https://x.com/9ranty/status/2115797158519550360

title: Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents
text:
Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic (https://simantic.com). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware.

Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes.

We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago.

To speed up the validation loop, we built the simulation layer that lets AI agents test the firmware and make decisions based on evidence, instead of waiting for the engineer to run tests for them. We used to spend hours testing our firmware manually on devboards, but now we use our own simulation to validate firmware in seconds.

What we offer: - Virtual devboards you can program and run with a single API call, without leaving your terminal. - An AI code reviewer for firmware, that makes informed decisions based on evidence, using our simulation as a verification engine. - A CI/CD pipeline for your hardware projects that validates your firmware against a simulated version of the microcontroller on every commit.

Here is a demo of our simulation used in an AI code review session: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ

Our users are using Simantic for bare-metal and RTOS development for applications like flight controllers, electric vehicles, robotics, and satellites. For safety critical systems like avionics and automotives, a robust simulation system is incredibly important, because every change in the firmware puts a human life at stake, especially for machines that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars.

We recently helped an early stage space startup building satellites, to test their firmware on hardware that they don't yet have. Even the development modules for those satellites costs over $100k, and we helped them do that at just a hundredth of the cost and time.

Early on in our journey, we established our idea to make better simulation but didn’t have a clear idea of how we would do it, we considered developing our software around open source emulation frameworks like Renode (https://github.com/renode/renode) and QEMU (https://www.qemu.org/), because they were tools already used within the firmware industry. We built our MVP that was essentially a wrapper around Renode, but we quickly realized there were a lot of limitations to doing this.

1. We were bottlenecked by the development speed of Renode themselves. We tried making contributions on Github to fix issues we came across, but the speed in which we could merge our features in was not fast enough for a startup like us trying to move fast.

2. Renode is built using Dotnet, and it was proving itself to be slower than we would have liked. Renode was released in 2017, which was when all code was still being written by hand, so I think it made sense looking back, but there were limitations because of the language itself.

3. The open source tools were bloated, with features that we would never use. Yes, there were a breadth of features, but we had a lot of things we had to work around just because we couldn’t remove or change them. Users were complaining about simulation accuracy. Renode is an emulator at the core, but our users, especially those who are building systems where timing accuracy is crucial did not find the accuracy good enough to validate their firmware.

Because of these issues, we made our own simulation engine from scratch, fully written in Rust.

- Our simulation is focused on accuracy. Open source frameworks often focus on expandability and developer experience, which means there were a lot of tradeoffs made to prioritize a breadth of models rather than going deep into a set of select models.

- We have our own hardware validation rigs running 24/7 to ensure our simulation models are as close to real world hardware as possible, and any gaps are detected and fixed as soon as we can. It currently looks like devboards connected to a Saleae Logic MSO and a SWD bus, controlled by a Linux PC, running Claude 24/7 just finding these gaps.

Our cloud-hosted simulator is available to use right now! We also provide a native binary with our developer plan licenses that let you run your firmware on your machines locally without any limitations.

Check it out at https://simantic.com/cloud-sim, and you can start using our AI firmware reviewer bot in your own Github repos here: https://simantic.com/dashboard/simantic-bot.

We currently have support for some models of the STM32F0, F4, H7 series MCUs, ESP32-S3/C3, and RP2040, but we’re constantly working to release new models every week, and improve our existing ones.

Thank you, and if you have any questions, feel free to send us an email at founders@simantic.dev

title: Show HN: StrictLLM – For when you need human-in-the-loop
text:

We've been working on this for the last 9 months and are nervcited to share this on HN and gather input.

StrictLLM is a desktop application for Mac, Windows, and Linux that will give you the following abilities:

- Human-in-the-loop with a strong focus in security and control

- Permissions enforced by code rather than a prompt

- Being able to talk to multiple AIs in the same conversation thread

- You can pull in any personas by @Mentions.

- Local and cloud models supported (OpenAI API Compatible and Anthropic Compatible)

- - LM Studio, Lemonade Server, Ollama, Claude, Strata, ChatGPT, OpenRouter, Kilo Gateway, etc. List is not exhaustive
